screens.title: Verifying Contracts on Etherscan
screens.subtitle: Prove the source of your deployed bytecode and unlock transparency, interaction, and easier auditing.

narration.text: When you deploy a smart contract it becomes bytecode on the chain, and that bytecode by itself is hard to interpret. Verifying a contract on a block explorer means uploading the original Solidity source and compilation settings so the explorer can recompile and confirm the deployed bytecode matches. That step produces a verified source view so users, auditors, and integrators can read your code and use a generated read/write interface. In practice, verification builds trust and reduces friction: users can inspect logic before interacting, auditors can review the exact code that runs on-chain, and anyone can call public functions from the explorer without a custom UI. In this chapter you will learn how to use the Hardhat Etherscan plugin, how to store and provide your Etherscan A P I key, how to pass constructor arguments correctly, and how to troubleshoot common mismatches such as optimizer or compiler differences. By the end you will be able to verify a deployed Counter contract on Sepolia and explain why verification matters for dApp adoption. Ask yourself: how would a missing verification influence a user’s decision to trust your dApp?

keyIdea.text: Verification proves that deployed bytecode corresponds to readable source, creating transparency and enabling the explorer’s read/write UI.

Second, you will learn to install and configure the Hardhat Etherscan plugin so verification can be automated from your development environment. Third, you will identify the exact configuration values required for a bytecode match — the compiler version, optimizer settings, and constructor arguments — and how to store an Etherscan A P I key securely. Each objective is grounded in practical steps you can apply immediately, and together they let you move from deploying a contract to making it transparent and usable for others. screens.title: What is Contract Verification?
screens.subtitle: Definition, purpose, and a trust-building example

narration.text: Contract verification is the formal process of supplying a contract’s original Solidity source code and compilation settings to a block explorer so it can recompile and compare the result to the bytecode that’s deployed on chain. The goal is a bytecode match: if Etherscan compiles the uploaded source with the same compiler version and optimizer settings and the resulting bytecode equals the on-chain bytecode, the explorer marks the source as verified. That simple proof unlocks multiple capabilities: humans can read the code, auditors can review it precisely, and the explorer can generate a read/write UI for interacting with public functions. A concrete example: you deploy a token contract to Sepolia. Without verification a user sees only the address and bytecode; with verification they can open the Code tab, read the transfer logic, and confirm there are no hidden owner-only mint functions. A common misconception is that verification changes the deployed contract or increases its privileges. It does not: verification is only a metadata assertion and a matching process. As a takeaway, verification acts as a transparency certificate — it doesn’t alter runtime behavior but it enables others to understand and trust the contract.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Verification proves that the uploaded source compiles to the deployed bytecode, making the contract readable and auditable.

Supply the original Solidity source and compile settings so an explorer recompiles and confirms a bytecode match against the deployed contract.

Why it matters

Misconception
Verification does not change on-chain behavior; it only proves source ↔ bytecode equivalence.
Example: Token on Sepolia

If you deploy a token and verify the contract, users can read the transfer logic and confirm there are no hidden mint paths. Without verification they must trust the dApp's claim about the contract's code.

Key Takeaway
Key Takeaway

screens.title: Benefits of Verification: Transparency vs Convenience
screens.subtitle: How verification helps users, auditors, and integrators

narration.text: Verification delivers multiple benefits that often fall into two practical categories: transparency and convenience. Transparency means anyone can read the source and reason about safety, permissions, and economic behavior. For example, a user checking an NFT contract can confirm whether a function allows the owner to freeze transfers. That trust is especially critical in DeFi and wallets where users deposit funds. Convenience refers to the explorer-generated interfaces: once verified, Etherscan exposes a Read/Write Contract UI so non-developers can call public functions without a custom front-end. This is helpful for quick audits, debugging, or interacting with contracts during testing. A common contrast is between an unverified contract that shows only bytecode and a verified contract that shows readable code plus function inputs. Many learners assume verification increases security automatically; it does not change the runtime guarantee. Instead, it makes manual auditing and automated tooling easier, which often leads to better security practices. As a takeaway, verification multiplies trust and reduces friction, but it is complementary to proper audits and testing. In practical terms, how verification helps users, auditors, and integrators. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Install and Configure the Hardhat Etherscan Plugin
screens.subtitle: Plugin installation, requiring it, and adding API key to config

narration.text: Hardhat offers a plugin that automates verification against Etherscan. The installation step is straightforward: add @nomicfoundation/hardhat-etherscan as a dev dependency to your project. After installation, require the plugin in your hardhat. config. js so the verify task becomes available. The plugin relies on an Etherscan A P I key for authenticated requests; obtain this key from Etherscan and store it as an environment variable, for example ETHERSCAN_API_KEY in your. env file. In your hardhat. config. js, add an etherscan object pointing to process. env. ETHERSCAN_API_KEY so the plugin picks it up. A concrete example from configuration shows requiring the toolbox and dotenv, setting solidity to the correct version, and adding the etherscan. apiKey mapping. A frequent misconception is to hardcode the A P I key in source — avoid this. Use environment variables and never commit your. env to source control. As a takeaway, the plugin converts verification into a reproducible CLI step, but it depends on secure A P I key management and a correct configuration to reproduce the deployment compilation environment. Install and Configure the Hardhat Etherscan Plugin means install the plugin, require it in config, and provide an environment-stored etherscan api key for automated verification.. In practical terms, plugin installation, requiring it, and adding api key to config. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Setup
keyIdea.text: Install the plugin, require it in config, and provide an environment-stored Etherscan API key for automated verification.

content.html:
Process Flow › Install and Configure Plugin
Steps
  1. Run npm install --save-dev @nomicfoundation/hardhat-etherscan in your project.
  2. Require the plugin and dotenv in hardhat.config.js so environment variables are available.
  3. Add an etherscan object with apiKey: process.env.ETHERSCAN_API_KEY to your module.exports.
Security note: keep your API key in .env and never commit it.
Config example
// hardhat.config.js
require("@nomicfoundation/hardhat-toolbox"); // includes etherscan plugin
require("dotenv").config();

module.exports = {
  solidity: "0.8.20",
  networks: { /* ... */ },
  etherscan: {
    apiKey: process.env.ETHERSCAN_API_KEY,
  },
};
This example shows the minimal entries you need. If you used optimizer settings during deployment, include them under solidity.settings as well.

screens.title: hardhat.config.js: Compiler and Optimizer Settings
screens.subtitle: Why matching compilation settings is essential for a bytecode match

narration.text: Etherscan reproduces your contract bytecode by compiling the uploaded source with the exact compiler version and settings you originally used. That means the solidity. version and solidity. settings. optimizer entries in hardhat. config. js must match deployment. If you deployed with optimizer enabled and runs set to 200, verification must use the same setting; a mismatch will change the compiled bytecode and cause a verification failure. As a concrete example, your config might specify version 0.8.20 with optimizer enabled and runs 200. If you accidentally set version 0.8.19 or disable the optimizer, the compiled output will differ. A typical misconception is that minor version differences or optimizer toggles are harmless; they are not. Even a change in runs can affect how the optimizer rearranges code. In practice, keep a deployment log or embed compiler settings in your release notes. When in doubt, recompile locally with the same settings and confirm the produced bytecode matches the on-chain bytecode before verifying. This reduces guesswork and speeds up verification. hardhat.config.js: Compiler and Optimizer Settings means the solidity version and optimizer settings used for verification must exactly match those used during deployment to produce identical bytecode.. In practical terms, why matching compilation settings is essential for a bytecode match. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Compiler match
keyIdea.text: The solidity version and optimizer settings used for verification must exactly match those used during deployment to produce identical bytecode.

content.html:
Definition › Compiler & Optimizer Settings
Key settings
  • solidity.version must equal the deployed compiler version.
  • solidity.settings.optimizer.enabled should match deployment.
  • solidity.settings.optimizer.runs must be the same number used at compile time.
Misconception check: changing optimizer runs can alter bytecode structure and lead to mismatches.
Config snippet
solidity: {
  version: "0.8.20",
  settings: {
    optimizer: {
      enabled: true,
      runs: 200,
    }
  }
}
Record these settings at deployment time. If you used a different tool or custom compilation pipeline, capture the exact compiler and settings used there as well.

screens.title: Running the Hardhat Verify Command
screens.subtitle: Command syntax and how to pass constructor arguments correctly

narration.text: After deployment and configuration, use the Hardhat CLI verify task to send your source and settings to Etherscan. The command format is npx hardhat verify --network and so on. Strings must be quoted, numeric and address arguments should match the deployed encoding and order exactly. For example, npx hardhat verify --network sepolia 0xAbc... "My Token" "MTK" will verify a token contract whose constructor took two string arguments for name and symbol. If there is no constructor, omit extra arguments. A common pitfall is supplying arguments in the wrong order or forgetting to surround strings with quotes; both produce incorrect constructor encodings that prevent a bytecode match. Another subtle issue is passing arrays or complex types: they must be encoded in the same form expected by the constructor. As a practical tip, copy constructor arguments from your deployment script or artifacts instead of retyping them. The command simplifies verification but depends on exact argument encoding to succeed. Running the Hardhat Verify Command means use npx hardhat verify with the network, address, and exact constructor arguments; quoting strings and matching order matters.. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Verify command
keyIdea.text: Use npx hardhat verify with the network, address, and exact constructor arguments; quoting strings and matching order matters.

content.html:
Process Flow › Running the Verify Command
Syntax and rules
  • Use the network flag to point at the network where the contract is deployed.
  • Provide the deployed contract address exactly.
  • Supply constructor arguments in order and format; quote strings.
Tip: copy constructor args from deployment artifacts to avoid encoding mistakes.
Example command
npx hardhat verify --network sepolia 0xYourContractAddress "My Token" "MTK"
If verification fails with argument errors, check order, types, and quoting. For complex types use the same encoding used during deployment.

screens.title: Common Verification Failures and How to Read Errors
screens.subtitle: Diagnose constructor, compiler, and API key problems

narration.text: When verification fails Etherscan reports an error that usually points to the mismatch source. The three most common causes are incorrect constructor arguments, mismatched compiler version or optimizer settings, and missing or invalid A P I keys. Constructor argument errors occur when the provided values produce a different constructor-encoded input than the one included at deployment. A mismatch in compiler version or optimizer settings leads to bytecode that structurally differs. A P I key issues typically result in authentication errors before verification begins. To diagnose, first confirm the contract address and that it’s on a public network — verification cannot run for local network addresses. Next, check the error message: if it references bytecode mismatch, re-check compiler and optimizer; if it complains about constructor encoding, re-evaluate argument order and quoting. A useful strategy is to recompile locally with the same settings and compare the resulting bytecode to the on-chain bytecode from the block explorer. Remember: Etherscan’s messages are usually descriptive, so follow them systematically rather than changing many variables at once. Common Verification Failures and How to Read Errors means use error messages to target constructor, compiler/optimizer mismatches, or api key problems; recompile locally to compare bytecode when needed.. In practical terms, diagnose constructor, compiler, and api key problems. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Troubleshoot
keyIdea.text: Use error messages to target constructor, compiler/optimizer mismatches, or API key problems; recompile locally to compare bytecode when needed.

content.html:
Core Concept › Common Verification Failures
Typical errors
  • Constructor encoding mismatch — check order and quoting.
  • Bytecode mismatch due to compiler or optimizer differences.
  • API key missing or invalid — verification requests fail early.
Diagnostic approach: verify network and address, then follow the error message to the likely root cause.
Practical check
  1. Confirm contract is deployed to a public network (Sepolia/Mainnet).
  2. Copy constructor args from deployment artifacts and re-run verification.
  3. Match compiler version and optimizer settings in hardhat.config.js.
Common mistake

Rushing to change settings without reproducing the original compile environment can prolong troubleshooting.

screens.title: Etherscan API Key and Secure Storage
screens.subtitle: Where to get the API key and how to keep it safe

narration.text: The Etherscan A P I key is required by the Hardhat plugin to submit verification requests. You obtain this key by registering an account with Etherscan and creating an A P I key; then set it as an environment variable in your project, for example ETHERSCAN_API_KEY in a. env file. The plugin reads process. env. ETHERSCAN_API_KEY so your key never needs to be checked into version control. Never hardcode the A P I key in your code or commit it to a public repository. A practical example: add ETHERSCAN_API_KEY="YOUR_API_KEY" to. env and make sure. gitignore includes. env. A common misconception is that the A P I key is optional; without it the plugin cannot authenticate requests and verification will fail. If you work in a team or CI environment, store the A P I key in CI secrets and inject it into the environment at runtime rather than embedding it in config files. As a takeaway, treat the A P I key like any other secret: store it securely, avoid exposing it, and scope its use to verification-related operations. Etherscan API Key and Secure Storage means obtain an etherscan api key and store it securely in environment variables; never hardcode or commit the key.. In practical terms, where to get the api key and how to keep it safe. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: API key
keyIdea.text: Obtain an Etherscan API key and store it securely in environment variables; never hardcode or commit the key.

content.html:
Definition › Etherscan API Key & Secure Storage
Where it comes from

Create an account on Etherscan and generate an API key; the same key works for supported testnets.

Add ETHERSCAN_API_KEY to .env and reference it via process.env in hardhat.config.js.
Security best practices
  • Never hardcode the API key into source files.
  • Add .env to .gitignore and use CI secrets for automated pipelines.
  • Restrict key usage and rotate if compromised.

screens.title: Verification Scope: Public Networks Only
screens.subtitle: When and where verification is possible

narration.text: Verification is performed by public block explorers, so only contracts deployed to public networks like Sepolia or Mainnet can be verified. Local chains such as a local Hardhat Network used for development do not have a corresponding public explorer and therefore cannot be verified on Etherscan. This matters because verification attempts against local addresses will fail or be meaningless; the explorer cannot access private networks. A practical example: if you deploy a Counter contract to Sepolia using npx hardhat run scripts/deploy_counter. js --network sepolia, you can then use the verify task against the Sepolia explorer. If you deploy locally using npx hardhat node and then deploy to that local network, Etherscan has no record of that chain state and cannot accept verification. Also confirm the contract address you pass to the verify command matches the deployed address — an incorrect address will produce a failure unrelated to compilation settings. As a takeaway, only public deployments can be verified; plan your release pipeline accordingly so verification happens after a public deployment step. Verification Scope: Public Networks Only means etherscan verification works only for contracts on public networks like sepolia or mainnet; local networks cannot be verified.. In practical terms, when and where verification is possible. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Scope

screens.title: Common Assessment & Troubleshooting Scenarios
screens.subtitle: Practice questions and targeted debugging steps

narration.text: To consolidate your learning, work through a few common scenarios you might encounter. Scenario one: you visit a dApp and the Code tab says "Contract Source Code Not Verified". Ask what you cannot see and why that matters — you cannot confirm the actual logic behind transactions, which reduces trust. Scenario two: your verify command returns a bytecode mismatch even though constructor args look correct. In that case, re-check your hardhat. config. js solidity. version and optimizer settings, and recompile locally to compare bytecode. Scenario three: the CLI reports an authentication error; confirm your ETHERSCAN_API_KEY is set in environment and not expired or disabled. For practice, attempt to verify a simple Counter contract, intentionally change a single config value and observe the error, then restore the original setting to see verification succeed. A useful misconception to correct: believing verification makes a contract safer automatically — it simply enables inspection and tooling that support better security practices. Finish by reflecting: which debugging step would you run first when verification fails? Why is an unverified contract a concern for users? They cannot read the code or confirm what the contract does.

Assessment Q2

If verification fails with a bytecode mismatch, what two config items should you check? Compiler version and optimizer settings.

Debugging Task

Intentionally change optimizer runs, attempt verification, then revert to observe the difference in errors and successful verification.

narration.text: Conclude with three practical points to carry forward. The Hardhat Etherscan Plugin automates verification tasks and requires installation and configuration in your project. The Etherscan A P I Key authenticates verification requests and must be stored as an environment secret rather than hardcoded. Constructor Arguments must be supplied exactly as they were encoded at deployment — wrong order or quoting is a leading cause of failures. Keep these three ideas top-of-mind as you verify contracts, and use systematic debugging: check the network and address first, then constructor args, then compiler and optimizer settings, and finally the A P I key if requests fail early.
